title: Neurosyphilis presenting with unusual hippocampal abnormalities on magnetic resonance imaging and positron emission tomography scans: a case report
case_prompt: A 55‐year‐old man was admitted after an unwitnessed collapse. Over the prior six months he had progressive memory difficulties. He was a smoker with no chronic illnesses and took no medications. On examination, vital signs were normal. His score on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment was 24/30, with deficits in delayed recall, language fluency, and orientation. Laboratory hematological and biochemical tests and cardiovascular studies were normal. Electroencephalography showed nonspecific irregular slowing without epileptiform discharges. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated right frontal gliosis, likely old trauma. Brain MRI on hospital day 2 showed high T2 signal and atrophy in the right frontal area consistent with gliosis, plus bilateral mesial temporal T2 hyperintensity. Lumbar puncture revealed 16 white blood cells/μL (100% mononuclear), protein 77 mg/dL, normal glucose, and a negative Gram stain. Brain 18F‐FDG PET demonstrated a focus of intensely increased uptake limited to the head of the right hippocampus on a background of globally reduced cortical uptake.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis was considered due to the subacute cognitive decline and mesial temporal MRI changes — “In view of his burgeoning cognitive problems and MRI findings, the possibility of a paraneoplastic (PN) process was considered.”  
2. Herpes simplex encephalitis was considered given acute mesial temporal hyperintensity — “Acute hyperintensity may be seen in herpes simplex encephalitis…”  
3. Vasculitis was considered because it can produce acute mesial temporal T2 changes — “Acute hyperintensity may be seen in… vasculitis…”  
4. Status epilepticus was considered as a cause of acute hyperintensity — “Acute hyperintensity may be seen in… status epilepticus.”  
5. Focal seizure activity was excluded by a timely EEG and clinical assessment — “However, an EEG was completed within two hours of the PET scan and showed no evidence of seizure. Furthermore, there were no fluctuating cognitive findings or pattern of awareness to suggest seizure activity.”  
6. Seizure was also unlikely because the pattern of uptake was structural, not electric — “Finally, the hypermetabolism outlined exactly the hippocampal head suggesting a structural rather than electric abnormality.”  
7. Mesial temporal sclerosis and neurodegenerative disorders were considered in the differential for chronic hyperintensity and atrophy — “Chronic hyperintensity along with atrophy is commonly seen in mesial temporal sclerosis and neurodegenerative disorders.”
